Final schema: Invoice(InvoiceNo, CustName, CustCity), InvoiceLine(InvoiceNo, Item), City(CustCity, CityState). Three tables, no redundancy, every anomaly gone.

Two marks most candidates leave on the table

First, state the key at every stage. The examiner is checking that you understand why the key changed from InvoiceNo to (InvoiceNo, Item) at 1NF, since that change is what creates the partial dependency 2NF then removes.

Second, name the dependency you are removing before you remove it. Write "CustName is partially dependent on InvoiceNo" and then split. A pair of tables with no explanation earns the structure mark but not the reasoning mark.

A refinement if you want to go further: CustName really belongs in a Customer table of its own, since a customer with several invoices would otherwise repeat their name. The scenario as given does not force it, but saying so shows you are designing rather than pattern matching.

t15.prompt: Database architecture is the set of specifications, rules and processes that dictate how data is stored in a database and how it is accessed by the components of a system. It includes data types, relationships and naming conventions.
t15.solution:
Slide 20 adds two sentences worth quoting directly. The architecture "describes the organization of all database objects and how they work together", and it "affects integrity, reliability, scalability and performance". Those four qualities are a ready made list if a question asks what the architecture determines.

Third sentence: it "involves anything that defines the nature of the data, the structure of the data, or how the data flows". Nature, structure, flow. That triple is an easy way to hold the definition.

The three types

Slide 21 names them: centralized, client-server, and distributed. The client-server type is then developed into two tier and three tier over slides 25 to 31, so treat it as one type with two configurations rather than as two separate types.

Drill

  1. Define database architecture. The definition above, then add that it describes the organisation of all database objects and how they work together, and that it affects integrity, reliability, scalability and performance.
  2. State the four system qualities affected by the database architecture. Integrity, reliability, scalability, performance.
  3. Name the three types of database architecture. Centralized, client-server (in two tier and three tier configurations), and distributed.

t16.prompt: A centralized database architecture is a system where all data is stored, managed and accessed from a single central location, typically a powerful server or mainframe. All users and applications connect to this central system to retrieve or manipulate data.
t16.solution:
Four key features

  • Single point of control. All data operations are handled by one central server.
  • Simplified maintenance. Updates, backups and security policies are applied in one place.
  • Minimal data redundancy. Since all data resides in one location, duplication is reduced.
  • Consistent performance. Predictable response times due to centralized processing.

Advantages and limitations, from slide 24

AdvantageDescription
Easy to manageOne location simplifies administration
Strong securityCentral control over access and policies
Cost effectiveLower infrastructure costs than distributed systems
Reliable backupsEasier to implement backup and recovery plans
LimitationDescription
Single point of failureIf the server crashes, the entire system goes down
Scalability issuesHarder to handle large user loads or geographic expansion
Performance bottlenecksHigh traffic can slow down the system
Limited flexibilityNot ideal for organisations with multiple remote locations

The worked example on slide 23

A university where all student records, namely grades, registration and attendance, sit on a central server, and students and staff across departments reach it through connected terminals. Benefits: easy coordination, centralized updates, consistent data. Drawback: if the server fails, nobody can access the data.

Use the university example rather than inventing one. It is the lecturer's own, you attend one, and it lets you name concrete data such as results and course registration instead of talking about "records" in the abstract.

Drill

  1. Define a centralized database architecture and state its four key features. The definition and the four bullets above.
  2. State four advantages and four limitations of the centralized architecture. The two tables above, four rows each.
  3. With an example, explain the main weakness of a centralized architecture. The single point of failure. In a university where results, registration and attendance are all on one server, an outage stops every department at once, since no local copy exists anywhere to fall back on.

t17.prompt: A database server is the computer software managing a database, and a client is an application that requests information from a server. Each computer in a network is a node that can host one or more databases, and each node can act as a client, a server, or both, depending on the situation.
t17.solution:
The structure

Two tiers: the client application and the database server. Users interact through a GUI to communicate with the database server across a network via SQL. The slide's own example of a common implementation is a Microsoft Windows client program accessing a server database such as Oracle or SQL Server.

A direct connection occurs when a client connects to a server and accesses information from a database contained on that server. An indirect connection reaches the data through another node.

The two configurations, which is the examinable part

ConfigurationWhere the processing happensAlso called
Thin clientMost of the processing occurs on the server tierFat server
Fat clientMost of the processing occurs on the client machineThin server

Thin client equals fat server, and fat client equals thin server. The pairing is the answer: the adjective describes where the work is not. Write both names for each configuration and the mark is secure.

Slide 27 also shows a web based two tier arrangement, where the browser is the client and the database server sits behind a web server. Mention it if you are asked for a modern instance.

Drill

  1. Define a database server, a client and a node. The three definitions above, verbatim from the slide.
  2. Distinguish a thin client from a fat client configuration. In a thin client, also called a fat server, most processing occurs on the server tier and the client mainly presents results. In a fat client, also called a thin server, most processing occurs on the client machine and the server mainly stores and serves data.
  3. Describe the two tier client-server architecture, with an example. Two tiers, client and database server. Users interact through a GUI and communicate with the server over the network using SQL. Example: a Windows client program accessing an Oracle or SQL Server database.

t18.prompt: The client-server model expands to include a middle tier, the business tier, which is an application server housing the business logic.
t18.solution:
What the middle tier does, in the slide's words

It "relieves the client applications and database server of some of their processing duties by translating client calls into database queries and translating data from the database into client data in return". Consequently, the client and server never talk directly to one another.

That last sentence is the one to quote. It is the single structural difference between two tier and three tier, and every advantage of the three tier design follows from it.

The three tiers named

TierAlso calledResponsibility
1Presentation tier, the clientThe user interface. Collects input, displays results.
2Business tier, the application serverThe business logic. Translates client calls into database queries and results back into client data.
3Data tier, the database serverStores the data, executes queries, enforces integrity.

Why the separation is worth the extra machine

  • Security. Clients hold no database credentials and cannot reach the database directly, so an attacker who compromises a client still faces the middle tier.
  • Maintainability. A change to a business rule is deployed once, on the application server, rather than reinstalled on every client machine.
  • Scalability. The middle tier can be duplicated behind a load balancer and can pool database connections, so a thousand clients need not mean a thousand database sessions.
  • Reuse. A web front end, a mobile app and a reporting tool can all call the same business tier instead of each reimplementing the rules.

Slides 30 and 31 show the web based three tier arrangement, which is what nearly every modern web application is: browser, web or application server, database server.

Drill

  1. Describe the three tier client-server architecture. Name all three tiers with responsibilities, then quote the consequence: the client and server never talk directly to one another.
  2. What is the function of the middle tier? It houses the business logic, and relieves the client and the database server of processing by translating client calls into database queries and translating returned data into client data.
  3. State four advantages of three tier over two tier. Security, maintainability, scalability and reuse, one sentence each as above.

t19.prompt:
This is the lecturer's own question, put on slide 32 with no answer after it. Of everything on this page, learn this one first.

"List advantages of two-tier over three-tier client-server architecture."
t19.solution:
Read the question the right way round It asks what the two tier design does better. Most students have memorised why three tier is superior and answer the opposite question, losing the whole mark. The two tier architecture is simpler and shorter, and every one of its advantages comes from those two facts.

Six advantages

AdvantageWhy it holds
Simpler to design and buildOnly two components and one connection between them, so there is no middle tier to specify, code or deploy. Development is faster and needs a smaller team.
Lower costNo application server to buy, license, host or maintain. Fewer machines and less software.
Faster response for a small user baseThe client speaks straight to the database, so a request crosses the network once instead of twice. Removing the middle tier removes its latency.
Easier to administer and troubleshootWith only two tiers there are fewer places a fault can hide, and a failure is localised to the client or the server immediately.
Direct access to database featuresThe client can use the DBMS's own tools, stored procedures and utilities directly, rather than through whatever the middle tier chooses to expose.
Well suited to small, stable, in-house applicationsFor a department sized system on one local network with a fixed set of users, the extra tier adds complexity without adding value.

How to finish the answer

Close with one sentence of balance, because it shows judgement and costs a line: these advantages hold only at small scale; as user numbers, security requirements or the number of client types grow, the three tier design overtakes it, since the middle tier is what allows business logic to be changed in one place and clients to be kept away from the database.

If the paper instead asks the question the other way round, the answer is T18: security, maintainability, scalability and reuse.

Drill

  1. List advantages of two tier over three tier client-server architecture. The six above.
  2. Under what circumstances would you choose a two tier architecture? A small, stable user base on a single local network, a single type of client application, an in-house system with modest security requirements, and a limited budget. The moment several client types, remote users or strict access control appear, choose three tier.
  3. Why does adding a middle tier increase latency? Because each request crosses the network twice, from client to application server and from application server to database, and is translated at the middle tier in both directions, instead of travelling once directly.

t20.prompt: A distributed database is a database stored across multiple physical locations, often on different servers or data centres, but which appears to users as a single unified system.
t20.solution:
The clause that earns the mark is the last one: it appears to the user as one system. If your definition stops at "stored in several places" you have described a set of separate databases, not a distributed one. Transparency is the whole idea.

Four key components

  • Sites or nodes. Independent systems that store parts of the database.
  • Data fragmentation. Splitting data into pieces, horizontally or vertically. Horizontal fragmentation divides by rows, such as one branch's customers per site; vertical divides by columns, such as payroll attributes held apart from personal details.
  • Replication. Copying data across multiple sites for reliability.
  • Middleware. Software that manages communication and query processing between sites.

The five types, slide 34, with the slide's own examples

TypeDescriptionExample
HomogeneousAll sites use the same DBMS and schemaA bank using Oracle DB in all its branches across Nigeria
HeterogeneousSites use different DBMSs or schemasA logistics firm using MySQL for inventory, MongoDB for tracking and PostgreSQL for billing
Client-serverA central server manages the data, clients send queriesAn enterprise HR system accessed from remote offices
Peer to peerAll nodes act as both client and serverBlockchain based distributed ledgers
FederatedIndependent databases linked by a common interfaceUniversities sharing student records across different systems

Advantages and challenges, slide 35

AdvantagesChallenges
Improved reliability and availabilityComplexity in design and management
Scalability across regionsSecurity risks across networks
Local autonomy for branch level operationsData consistency and synchronisation issues
Faster query processing through parallelism

Each advantage is the mirror of a centralized limitation, which is a useful way to answer a "compare" question: no single point of failure because the data lives in several places, geographic scalability because a new region gets a new site, and faster queries because sites work in parallel rather than queueing at one server.

Drill

  1. Define a distributed database and state its four key components. The definition, ending on "appears as a single unified system", then sites, fragmentation, replication and middleware.
  2. Differentiate homogeneous from heterogeneous distributed databases, with an example of each. Homogeneous: every site runs the same DBMS and schema, such as a bank running Oracle in all Nigerian branches. Heterogeneous: sites run different DBMSs or schemas, such as a logistics firm on MySQL, MongoDB and PostgreSQL. The heterogeneous case needs middleware to translate between systems, which the homogeneous case does not.
  3. Compare centralized and distributed architectures. Centralized: one location, easy to manage and secure, cheaper, but a single point of failure that scales badly. Distributed: several sites appearing as one system, reliable, regionally scalable, faster through parallelism and locally autonomous, but complex to manage, exposed across networks, and hard to keep consistent.
  4. What is data fragmentation, and name its two forms. Splitting the database into pieces stored at different sites. Horizontal fragmentation divides by rows, vertical fragmentation divides by columns.

t21.prompt: Slides 36 to 39, the last content in the deck. Developing a database application involves a series of well defined steps to ensure the system meets user needs, maintains data integrity and performs efficiently. This is the Database Development Life Cycle (DDLC).
t21.solution:
#StageWhat happens, from the slides
1Requirement analysisUnderstand what users need. Interview stakeholders, identify data types, relationships and workflows, document functional and non-functional requirements.
2Conceptual designTool: ER modelling. Output: ER diagrams showing entities, attributes and relationships. Goal: a high level blueprint of the data structure.
3Logical designConvert the ER model to a relational model. Define tables, keys and constraints, normalize to reduce redundancy, apply relational algebra for query logic.
4Physical designHow data will be stored and accessed. Indexing strategies, storage formats, performance optimisation.
5ImplementationTools: SQL, MS Access, MySQL, PostgreSQL. Create tables, views and stored procedures, develop queries, forms and reports, integrate with front end applications.
6Testing and validationUnit testing of individual components, integration testing system wide, and user acceptance testing. Goal: accuracy, performance and usability.
7DeploymentInstall on production servers, configure access controls and security, train users and provide documentation.
8Maintenance and updatesMonitor performance, apply patches and updates, modify the schema as business needs evolve.

Stages 2, 3 and 4 map exactly onto the conceptual, logical and physical models of R3. That is not a coincidence, and saying so in an answer connects two topics for free.

The three kinds of testing, since they are separately markable

  • Unit testing checks one component in isolation, such as a single stored procedure or a validation rule.
  • Integration testing checks the system as a whole, that the parts work together once connected.
  • User acceptance testing (UAT) checks that the users agree the system does what they asked for. It is the only one of the three the users themselves perform.

Drill

  1. List and explain the eight stages of the database development life cycle. The table above, one or two sentences each.
  2. What happens during requirement analysis? Stakeholders are interviewed to establish what they need from the database, the data types, relationships and workflows are identified, and both functional and non-functional requirements are documented.
  3. Differentiate conceptual, logical and physical design in the DDLC. Conceptual design produces the ER diagram as a high level blueprint. Logical design converts it to a relational model, defining tables, keys and constraints, and normalizes it. Physical design decides how the data is actually stored and accessed, covering indexing, storage formats and performance tuning.
  4. Name three types of testing and state who performs each. Unit testing of individual components and integration testing across the system are performed by developers and testers; user acceptance testing is performed by the users themselves.
  5. Why does the life cycle not end at deployment? Because business needs change. Maintenance covers monitoring performance, applying patches and updates, and modifying the schema as requirements evolve, so the cycle continues for the working life of the system.

t22.prompt: Outline item 6. Relational algebra is a formal query language: a set of operators that each take one or two relations and return a relation. Because the output is itself a relation, operators can be composed, which is what makes it an algebra.
t22.solution:
The operators

OperatorSymbolWhat it doesSQL equivalent
Selectσ (sigma)Chooses the rows that satisfy a conditionWHERE
Projectπ (pi)Chooses the columns, and removes duplicate rows from the resultSELECT DISTINCT
Union∪All rows in either relation, duplicates removedUNION
Intersection∩Rows present in both relationsINTERSECT
Difference−Rows in the first relation and not in the secondEXCEPT
Cartesian product×Every row of one paired with every row of the otherCROSS JOIN
Join⋈A Cartesian product followed by a selection on the matching conditionINNER JOIN
Renameρ (rho)Renames a relation or its attributesAS

The distinction examiners test most: select takes rows, project takes columns. The names are counterintuitive because SQL's keyword SELECT does the job of relational algebra's project. Say that explicitly and you have shown you know both.

Union compatibility

Union, intersection and difference require the two relations to be union compatible: the same number of attributes, with corresponding attributes drawn from the same domains. Select, project, product and join carry no such requirement.

Worked examples on the university schema from T9

  • Students born before 2005: σDateOfBirth < '2005-01-01'(Student)
  • Just the names and matriculation numbers: πMatricNo, Name(Student)
  • Names of students who scored an A: πName(σGrade='A'(Student ⋈ Enrolment))

Read the third one from the inside out, because that is the order the operations happen: join Student to Enrolment, keep only the A rows, then keep only the Name column. Writing the expression in that order in the exam earns the working marks even if the notation slips.

Drill

  1. Define relational algebra and state why it is called an algebra. A formal query language of operators that take relations as input and produce relations as output; it is an algebra because the closure property, output being the same type as input, allows operators to be composed into expressions.
  2. Differentiate the select operator from the project operator. Select (σ) filters rows against a condition and keeps every column; project (π) keeps named columns for every row and eliminates duplicates from the result. One works horizontally, the other vertically.
  3. Write relational algebra to list the names of all students enrolled in CS101. πName(σCourseCode='CS101'(Student ⋈ Enrolment)).
  4. What does union compatibility mean, and which operators require it? Two relations are union compatible when they have the same number of attributes and corresponding attributes are from the same domains. Union, intersection and difference require it.

t23.prompt: Outline items 7 and 8. SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for defining, manipulating and controlling data in a relational database. It is declarative: you state what you want, and the DBMS decides how to get it.
t23.solution:
The four sublanguages, a guaranteed recall question

SublanguageStands forStatementsActs on
DDLData Definition LanguageCREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATEThe structure: tables, views, indexes
DMLData Manipulation LanguageSELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETEThe rows inside the tables
DCLData Control LanguageGRANT, REVOKEPermissions
TCLTransaction Control LanguageCOMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINTTransaction boundaries

The trap: DELETE is DML and TRUNCATE is DDL, even though both empty a table. DELETE removes rows one at a time, fires triggers and can be rolled back; TRUNCATE drops and recreates the structure, so it is faster and generally cannot be undone.

The statements you should be able to write from memory

Creating a table with its constraints, which is where entity and referential integrity from T9 stop being theory:

CREATE TABLE Student (
MatricNo    VARCHAR(15) PRIMARY KEY,
Name        VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL,
DateOfBirth DATE
);
CREATE TABLE Enrolment (
MatricNo   VARCHAR(15),
CourseCode VARCHAR(8),
Grade      CHAR(1),
PRIMARY KEY (MatricNo, CourseCode),
FOREIGN KEY (MatricNo)   REFERENCES Student(MatricNo),
FOREIGN KEY (CourseCode) REFERENCES Course(CourseCode)
);

Querying across two tables:

SELECT s.Name, e.CourseCode, e.Grade
FROM   Student s
JOIN   Enrolment e ON s.MatricNo = e.MatricNo
WHERE  e.Grade = 'A'
ORDER  BY s.Name;

Changing and removing rows, always with a WHERE clause:

INSERT INTO Student (MatricNo, Name, DateOfBirth)
VALUES ('CS/2022/001', 'Alex', '2004-03-11');
UPDATE Enrolment SET Grade = 'B'
WHERE  MatricNo = 'CS/2022/001' AND CourseCode = 'CS101';
DELETE FROM Enrolment
WHERE  MatricNo = 'CS/2022/001';

An UPDATE or DELETE written without a WHERE clause changes every row in the table. In an exam it costs marks; in production it costs the data.

The clause order, which is also the marking order

SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY. Written in that order, executed in roughly the opposite: the source is read, rows are filtered, groups are formed, groups are filtered, columns are chosen, and the result is sorted last.

Drill

  1. State the four categories of SQL statement with two examples of each. The table above.
  2. Write SQL to create the Enrolment table with its primary and foreign keys. The CREATE TABLE above.
  3. Write SQL to list every student's name alongside the courses they are enrolled in. A join of Student and Enrolment on MatricNo, selecting Name and CourseCode.
  4. Differentiate DELETE from TRUNCATE, and DROP from DELETE. DELETE removes rows and can be rolled back; TRUNCATE removes all rows by recreating the table and generally cannot; DROP removes the table itself, structure and all.

t24.prompt: Outline item 9, listed separately from SQL itself, which usually means it carries its own question. Functions divide into aggregate functions, which collapse many rows into one value, and scalar functions, which transform one value into another.
t24.solution:
The five aggregate functions

FunctionReturnsNote
COUNT()Number of rowsCOUNT(*) counts every row; COUNT(col) skips nulls in that column
SUM()Total of a numeric columnIgnores nulls
AVG()Mean of a numeric columnIgnores nulls, so it is not always sum divided by row count
MIN()Smallest valueWorks on numbers, dates and text
MAX()Largest valueWorks on numbers, dates and text

Scalar functions, by family

  • String: UPPER(), LOWER(), LENGTH(), SUBSTRING(), CONCAT(), TRIM().
  • Numeric: ROUND(), CEIL(), FLOOR(), ABS(), MOD().
  • Date: NOW(), CURDATE(), YEAR(), MONTH(), DATEDIFF().
  • Null handling: COALESCE(), which returns the first non-null argument, and IFNULL() or NVL() depending on the DBMS.

GROUP BY and HAVING

An aggregate over the whole table returns one row. GROUP BY makes it return one row per group instead:

SELECT   CourseCode, COUNT(*) AS Enrolled, AVG(Score) AS MeanScore
FROM     Enrolment
GROUP BY CourseCode
HAVING   COUNT(*) > 10
ORDER BY MeanScore DESC;

The most tested distinction in this topic: WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after. This is why an aggregate function may appear in HAVING but never in WHERE: at the time WHERE runs, the groups do not yet exist.

The other rule: every column in the SELECT list must either appear in the GROUP BY clause or be wrapped in an aggregate function. Selecting a bare column that is not grouped is the classic error.

Drill

  1. Name five aggregate functions and state what each returns. The table above.
  2. Differentiate WHERE from HAVING. WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping takes place, so it cannot reference an aggregate. HAVING filters the groups produced by GROUP BY after aggregation, so it can.
  3. Write SQL to show each course and its average score, listing only courses with more than ten students. The query above.
  4. Why can COUNT(*) and COUNT(column) return different numbers? Because COUNT(*) counts every row while COUNT(column) counts only rows where that column is not null.

t25.prompt: Outline items 7 and 10. A transaction is a logical unit of work made up of one or more operations that must either all succeed or all fail, leaving the database consistent either way. The standard example is a bank transfer: debit one account, credit another, and never do one without the other.
t25.solution:
ACID, the certainty on this paper

PropertyMeaningOn the transfer example
AtomicityAll operations complete or none doIf the credit fails, the debit is rolled back. Money never vanishes in transit.
ConsistencyThe database moves from one valid state to another, with all constraints satisfiedTotal money across both accounts is unchanged.
IsolationConcurrent transactions do not interfere; each behaves as though it ran aloneA balance enquiry running at the same time never sees the debit without the credit.
DurabilityOnce committed, changes survive any subsequent failureAfter the commit, a power cut cannot undo the transfer.

Give the transfer example for all four. One scenario carried through the whole answer reads far better than four unrelated illustrations, and it is faster to write.

The three concurrency problems

  • Lost update. Two transactions read the same value and both write back; the second overwrites the first, whose update is lost. Two clerks selling the last seat is the standard case.
  • Dirty read, or uncommitted dependency. A transaction reads a value another has written but not yet committed. If that transaction then rolls back, the first has acted on data that never officially existed.
  • Inconsistent analysis, or non-repeatable read. A transaction reads several rows while another is updating them, so its results reflect a mixture of before and after, and a total does not balance.

How they are prevented

  • Locking. A shared lock permits other readers but no writers; an exclusive lock permits neither. Two phase locking requires that a transaction acquires all the locks it needs before releasing any, which is what guarantees serialisability.
  • Timestamp ordering. Each transaction receives a timestamp and conflicting operations are forced into that order, so no locks are needed.
  • Deadlock. Two transactions each hold a lock the other wants, so neither can proceed. It is handled by prevention, ordering lock acquisition so a cycle cannot form, or by detection, in which the DBMS finds the cycle and aborts one transaction as the victim, rolling it back so the other can continue.

A serialisable schedule is one whose effect is the same as some serial execution of the same transactions one after another. That is the correctness standard concurrency control aims at: the speed of running transactions at the same time, with the result of having run them one by one.

Drill

  1. Define a transaction and explain the ACID properties. The definition plus the four rows, illustrated with the bank transfer.
  2. State three problems that arise from concurrent access. Lost update, dirty read, inconsistent analysis, each with its one line scenario.
  3. What is a deadlock, and how is it resolved? A situation where two or more transactions each hold a lock the other needs, so none can proceed. It is resolved by prevention, by imposing an order on lock acquisition, or by detection, where the DBMS identifies the wait cycle and aborts and rolls back one transaction as the victim.
  4. Differentiate COMMIT from ROLLBACK. COMMIT makes every change in the transaction permanent and visible to other users. ROLLBACK undoes them all, returning the database to its state at the start of the transaction.

t26.prompt: Outline item 11. Database security is the protection of a database against threats to its confidentiality, integrity and availability, whether those threats are deliberate attacks, accidental damage or hardware failure.
t26.solution:
The CIA triad, which frames the whole answer

  • Confidentiality. Only authorised users can read the data. Enforced by authentication, authorisation, views and encryption.
  • Integrity. The data is accurate and can only be changed in permitted ways. Enforced by constraints, transactions and the audit trail.
  • Availability. Authorised users can reach the data when they need it. Enforced by backups, recovery procedures and redundancy.

The countermeasures worth naming

ControlWhat it does
AuthenticationEstablishes who the user is, by password, token or biometric
Authorisation and privilegesEstablishes what that user may do. GRANT and REVOKE assign privileges, ideally by role rather than to individuals
ViewsExpose a restricted window onto a table, so a clerk can see names without seeing salaries
EncryptionRenders data unreadable without the key, both at rest on disk and in transit across the network
Backup and recoveryKeeps a copy that can be restored, with a transaction log allowing recovery to a point in time
Audit trailRecords who did what and when, which deters misuse and makes investigation possible
Integrity constraintsPrevent invalid data being written in the first place

Two principles to quote: least privilege, meaning every user receives the minimum access their job requires and nothing more, and defence in depth, meaning no single control is trusted alone.

The threat everyone should be able to name

SQL injection occurs when user input is concatenated into a query string, letting an attacker change the meaning of the statement rather than merely supply a value. The defence is parameterised queries, or prepared statements, in which the input can never be parsed as SQL, backed by input validation and least privilege on the database account.

The architectural connection worth making: this is one reason the three tier design of T18 is more secure than two tier. Clients hold no database credentials at all, so a compromised client cannot query the database directly.

Drill

  1. State the three goals of database security. Confidentiality, integrity and availability, with one control named for each.
  2. Name five database security countermeasures and explain each. Any five rows of the table.
  3. What is SQL injection and how is it prevented? An attack in which user input is placed into a query so that it is interpreted as SQL rather than as data, allowing the attacker to alter the statement. It is prevented by parameterised queries or prepared statements, input validation, and granting the application account only the privileges it needs.
  4. Differentiate authentication from authorisation. Authentication verifies identity, establishing who the user is. Authorisation determines what that identified user is permitted to do. Authentication comes first; authorisation acts on its result.

t27.prompt: Outline item 14, and the only practical component. It is listed as four objects, which almost certainly means a four part question, one part per object.
t27.solution:
The four objects and what each is for

ObjectPurposeKey points to state
TableStores the data, one table per entityDesigned in Design View: field name, data type (Text, Number, Date/Time, Currency, Yes/No, AutoNumber), and field properties. Set the primary key here; relationships are drawn in the Relationships window and enforce referential integrity.
QueryRetrieves and manipulates dataBuilt in Query Design using QBE, query by example, or written in SQL View. Select queries read; action queries (update, append, delete, make-table) change data. Criteria go in the criteria row.
FormProvides the interface for entering and viewing recordsOne record at a time, which reduces data entry error compared with typing into a table. Controls can be bound to fields, and validation is applied at entry.
ReportFormats data for printing or presentationRead only. Supports grouping, sorting, and totals in group and report footers. Based on a table or, more usually, on a query.

The relationship between them is the answer to "how do these objects work together": tables hold the data, queries select from tables, forms enter data into tables, and reports present the output of queries. One sentence, four objects, all the marks.

Two further points that come up

Macros and modules are the remaining Access object types, automating tasks without code and with VBA code respectively. Name them if a question asks for all the object types rather than these four.

Access is a desktop DBMS. It suits a single user or a small workgroup, and its file has a size limit around two gigabytes. For many concurrent users or larger data, the tables move to a server DBMS such as SQL Server while Access is sometimes kept as the front end. That trade-off connects directly to the architectures of T17, and mentioning it shows the course as a whole rather than as separate topics.

Drill

  1. Name the four main MS Access objects and state the function of each. The table above.
  2. Explain how tables, queries, forms and reports relate to one another. Tables store the data; queries retrieve and manipulate what the tables hold; forms provide a controlled interface for entering and editing records in the tables; reports present the results, usually of a query, in printable form.
  3. Describe the steps to create a table and set a primary key in MS Access. Open the database, choose Create then Table, switch to Design View, enter each field name with its data type and properties, select the field that uniquely identifies a record, click Primary Key on the ribbon, then save the table with a name.
  4. What is the difference between a select query and an action query? A select query retrieves and displays data without changing it. An action query changes the data, and includes update, append, delete and make-table queries.

d1.prompt:
University schemas: Students(StudentID PK, Name, Major, EnrollmentDate), Courses(CourseID PK, Title, Department), Enrollment(StudentID PK, CourseID PK, Grade) (composite key).

a) Write SQL to: (i) retrieve Name and Major of all students in the Computer Science department (department is the student's Major); (ii) list the Title of all courses offered by the History department; (iii) increase Grade by 5 for all rows in Enrollment with Grade below 50. Show the syntax.

b) Explain the difference between internal, conceptual and external schema in the three-schema architecture. c) Define and relate: data, information, database, DBMS. d) (i) Describe the three-level architecture of a DBMS; (ii) for each level, name the typical users/processes and the schema type. e) (i) Outline the phases of the database system development life cycle; (ii) briefly describe the goal of each.
d1.solution:
a) The three SQL statements

(i) Students whose Major is Computer Science:

SELECT Name, Major
FROM   Students
WHERE  Major = 'Computer Science';

(ii) Titles of courses run by the History department:

SELECT Title
FROM   Courses
WHERE  Department = 'History';

(iii) Add 5 to every failing grade. This is an UPDATE, not a SELECT: the WHERE restricts which rows change.

UPDATE Enrollment
SET    Grade = Grade + 5
WHERE  Grade < 50;
  • Marks are lost here for forgetting the WHERE in (iii), which would raise every grade, and for quoting the number 50. String literals get quotes; numbers do not.

b) Internal, conceptual, external schema

These are the three levels of the ANSI-SPARC architecture, from the machine up to the user:

SchemaDescribesConcerned with
Internal (physical)how the data is physically storedfiles, indexes, storage layout
Conceptual (logical)what data is stored and its relationships, for the whole databaseentities, tables, constraints
External (view)the portion of the database a particular user group seesuser views, hiding the rest

The point of the split is data independence: you can change the internal storage without touching the conceptual schema (physical independence), and change the conceptual schema without touching most external views (logical independence).

c) Data, information, database, DBMS

  • Data: raw, unprocessed facts (the number 78, the name "Ada").
  • Information: data processed into a meaningful, useful form ("Ada scored 78 in CSC413").
  • Database: an organised, related collection of that data, stored so it can be retrieved.
  • DBMS: the software that defines, stores, retrieves and controls access to the database (Oracle, MySQL, MS Access).

Relationship: data becomes information once processed; a database stores the data in an organised way; and a DBMS is the tool that manages the database and turns stored data into information for users.

d) Three-level architecture, users and schemas

Same three levels as (b), now tagged with who works at each:

LevelSchemaTypical user / process
Externalexternal schema (views)end users, application programs
Conceptualconceptual schemadatabase administrator, designers
Internalinternal schemathe DBMS storage manager, the operating system

e) Database development life cycle

The main phases and the goal of each:

PhasePrimary goal
1. Requirements analysisgather what data and functions the users need
2. Conceptual designbuild the ER model, independent of any DBMS
3. Logical designmap the ER model to relational tables and normalise
4. Physical designchoose storage, indexes and file structures for a specific DBMS
5. Implementationcreate the database, load data, write applications
6. Testing and maintenanceverify, tune, and keep it running as needs change

Phases 2, 3 and 4 map onto the conceptual, logical and physical models of R3, which is worth stating for a free connecting mark.

d2.prompt: a) Briefly describe the primary functions of the database languages you know. b) Define: relation, tuple, attribute, domain, primary key. c) Describe the difference between full, incremental and differential backup, with examples of when each fits. d) Describe the client/server database model.
d2.solution:
a) Database languages

LanguageFunctionExample statements
DDL (Data Definition)defines the schema: create and alter structureCREATE, ALTER, DROP
DML (Data Manipulation)queries and changes the dataSELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
DCL (Data Control)grants and revokes access rightsGRANT, REVOKE
TCL (Transaction Control)manages transactionsCOMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT

b) Relational model terms

  • Relation: a table of rows and columns.
  • Tuple: one row of a relation (one record).
  • Attribute: one column of a relation (a named field).
  • Domain: the set of allowed values for an attribute (for example, Grade in 0 to 100).
  • Primary key: an attribute (or set) that uniquely identifies each tuple, and cannot be null.

c) Backup types

BackupWhat it copiesTrade-off
Fullthe entire database, every timeslowest to make, largest, but fastest and simplest to restore
Incrementalonly data changed since the last backup of any kindsmallest and fastest to make, but restore needs the full plus every increment in order
Differentialall data changed since the last full backupgrows each day, but restore needs only the full plus the latest differential

When each fits: a weekly full on Sunday, then incrementals nightly if backup time and storage are tight, or differentials nightly if fast restore matters more than storage.

d) Client/server database model

The database work is split between two roles. The server holds the database and the DBMS, and does the storage, query processing and concurrency control. The clients are the applications that send requests (SQL) over the network and receive results. One server serves many clients, which centralises the data (one authoritative copy, easier security and backup) while letting many users work at once. It contrasts with a single-user desktop database where one program owns the file directly.

d3.prompt: a) (i) Purpose of query processing; (ii) outline the query processing pipeline. b) Importance of query optimization. c) Explain Discretionary Access Control (DAC). d) (i) Describe the ACID properties; (ii) explain how ACID ensures integrity in a multi-user environment.
d3.solution:
a) Query processing

(i) Purpose: to translate a high-level query (SQL) into an efficient low-level execution plan and run it against the stored data to return the result.

(ii) Pipeline:

  1. Parsing and translation: check syntax and turn the SQL into relational algebra.
  2. Optimization: generate candidate execution plans and pick the cheapest by cost estimate.
  3. Evaluation (execution): the execution engine runs the chosen plan and returns the rows.

b) Why query optimization matters

The same query can be executed in many ways, and their costs differ by orders of magnitude (a full table scan versus an index lookup, or the join order chosen). Optimization picks the plan with the least estimated cost in disk I/O and CPU, so it directly decides response time, throughput and how many users the system can serve. On large tables it is the difference between milliseconds and minutes.

c) Discretionary Access Control

DAC is a security model in which access rights are granted at the discretion of the data owner. The owner of an object (a table, a view) decides which users get which privileges (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE) and can pass on the right to grant. In SQL this is exactly the GRANT and REVOKE mechanism. It is flexible, but because rights can be delegated freely it is weaker than mandatory access control, where a central policy fixes them.

d) ACID

PropertyGuarantee
Atomicitya transaction is all-or-nothing; partial effects are rolled back
Consistencya transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, honouring all constraints
Isolationconcurrent transactions do not interfere; each runs as if alone
Durabilityonce committed, changes survive crashes and power loss

(ii) In a multi-user environment, many transactions run at once and can collide (lost updates, dirty reads). Isolation (through locking or versioning) keeps them from seeing each other's uncommitted work; atomicity ensures a transaction that fails midway leaves no half-finished changes; consistency enforces the integrity rules throughout; and durability guarantees a committed result is not lost. Together they keep the shared data correct despite concurrency and failure.

d4.prompt: a) Three main properties of a secured database. b) DAC in the context of database security. c) (i) Differentiate a relational database from a NoSQL database; (ii) give two advantages and two disadvantages of each. d) Propose and justify a backup and recovery strategy for a hospital database that runs 24/7 with minimal downtime. e) List and explain four types of database user, with a real-world example of each.
d4.solution:
a) Properties of a secured database

The classic CIA triad: Confidentiality (only authorised users can read data), Integrity (data cannot be altered improperly), and Availability (the data is there when authorised users need it).

b) DAC in database security

As in Q3(c): the owner of each object controls who may access it, granting privileges per user and per operation with GRANT / REVOKE. In security terms, DAC implements confidentiality and integrity at fine grain (this clerk may read Patients but not update Billing), but its reliance on owner discretion and delegation means a careless grant can leak access, which is its main weakness.

c) Relational vs NoSQL

Relational (SQL)NoSQL
Data modeltables, fixed schemadocuments, key-value, column, graph; flexible schema
Scalingvertical (bigger server)horizontal (more servers)
Consistencystrong (ACID)often eventual (BASE)

Relational advantages: ACID guarantees; powerful, standard SQL querying. Disadvantages: rigid schema; harder to scale out horizontally. NoSQL advantages: flexible schema; scales horizontally for huge/varied data. Disadvantages: weaker consistency; no single standard query language.

d) Hospital backup and recovery, 24/7

A hospital cannot go offline and cannot lose records, so combine several techniques:

  • Online (hot) backups so the database keeps serving while it is backed up.
  • A weekly full backup plus daily differentials (or nightly incrementals) to bound both backup time and restore time.
  • Continuous transaction-log archiving to allow point-in-time recovery to the moment before a failure.
  • Replication to a standby server (and off-site copies) so that if the primary fails the standby takes over with near-zero downtime.

Justification: replication gives high availability (the 24/7 requirement); log archiving gives a tiny recovery-point (little or no data loss); and the full-plus-differential schedule keeps routine backups cheap without making recovery slow.

e) Four types of database user

UserRoleExample
Database administrator (DBA)creates the database, manages security, backup, tuningthe IT staffer who runs the bank's DBMS
Database designerdesigns the schema and constraintsthe analyst who models a new hospital system
Application programmerwrites programs that access the databasea developer building the mobile banking app
End userqueries and updates data through applicationsa bank teller entering a deposit

d5.prompt: a) Design a database for a university library storing books, students, staff and borrowing records. Each book can have multiple authors. A student can borrow multiple books but no more than five at a time. Staff reserve books but do not borrow them. (i) Draw the ER diagram; (ii) convert it to a relational schema; (iii) list the primary keys; (iv) show how foreign keys enforce the relationships. b) Explain with an example how deadlock can occur in a multi-user database. c) Suggest two techniques for deadlock prevention or recovery.
d5.solution:
(i) ER diagram, described

Entities and relationships to draw (rectangles for entities, diamonds for relationships, and note the cardinality on each line):

  • Book, Author, Student, Staff are entities.
  • Book M:N Author ("written by"): a book has many authors and an author writes many books.
  • Student M:N Book ("borrows"), with attributes BorrowDate and DueDate, and the business rule "at most five current loans per student".
  • Staff M:N Book ("reserves"), with a ReserveDate. Staff reserve but never borrow, so there is no Staff-to-borrows line.

(ii) Relational schema

Each entity becomes a table; each M:N relationship becomes its own junction table carrying the two keys plus any relationship attributes.

Student(StudentID, Name, Level)
Staff(StaffID, Name, Department)
Book(BookID, Title, ISBN, Copies)
Author(AuthorID, Name)
BookAuthor(BookID, AuthorID)
Borrow(StudentID, BookID, BorrowDate, DueDate)
Reserve(StaffID, BookID, ReserveDate)

(iii) Primary keys

TablePrimary key
StudentStudentID
StaffStaffID
BookBookID
AuthorAuthorID
BookAuthor(BookID, AuthorID) composite
Borrow(StudentID, BookID, BorrowDate) composite
Reserve(StaffID, BookID) composite

(iv) Foreign keys enforcing the relationships

  • In BookAuthor, BookID references Book and AuthorID references Author, so an author link can only name a book and an author that exist. That is what makes the M:N "written by" real.
  • In Borrow, StudentID references Student and BookID references Book, so a loan cannot name a non-existent student or book. The five-book limit is enforced by application logic or a trigger counting current rows per StudentID.
  • In Reserve, StaffID references Staff and BookID references Book. Because only Staff appears here, the design itself prevents a student from reserving and a staff member from borrowing.

This is referential integrity: a foreign key value must match an existing primary key in the referenced table, or be null.

b) How deadlock occurs

Deadlock is when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs, so neither can proceed. Example: transaction T1 locks row A and then asks for row B; at the same moment T2 has locked row B and asks for row A. T1 waits for T2, T2 waits for T1, and they wait forever. In a library: T1 (a return) locks the Book row then wants the Borrow row; T2 (a renewal) locks the Borrow row then wants the Book row.

c) Two techniques

  • Deadlock prevention by lock ordering: require every transaction to acquire locks in the same global order (always Book before Borrow), so the circular wait cannot form.
  • Deadlock detection and recovery: the DBMS maintains a wait-for graph, detects a cycle, and aborts (rolls back) one transaction, the "victim", to break it, then restarts it. Timeouts are a simpler variant.
